title: prompts.chat
same: Every counted sample's results were read from its own job logs. In all 10 counted samples (5 per configuration) the same 3 jobs ran and passed, with the same 203 checks, all passing: `Test` in `ci.yml` (`npm ci`, ESLint, and the 95 Vitest test files and their total), `test` in `docker-publish.yml` (`npm ci` and the same 95 Vitest files and total, which gate the image), and `build-and-push`, which built the Docker image for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (for each CPU type: the dependency install, the Next.js build, the Prisma CLI install and the finished image). The image build is checked by those steps completing, not by comparing images byte for byte. With the agent PR, the Next.js app is built once, on the runner's own CPU, and that one build goes into both images; each image still gets its own CPU's Prisma client. The images are built but not published.
notes: **Control configuration.** Each round also replayed the event on StarSling runners with the CI unchanged, as an internal control. It is not part of this comparison, and its samples are not shown on this page.

**Lane: merges to the default branch.** This page measures merges to prompts.chat's default branch. The default branch is `main`. Each sample replays the merge of `1dc18fd9`. PR updates were not measured: at this commit `ci.yml` also runs on pull requests, but `docker-publish.yml`, which builds the image, runs only on merges to the default branch, version tags and manual runs, and no upstream pull request was pinned for replay.

**Workflows in this merge.** The replayed merge runs `ci.yml` (`Test`: install, lint, Vitest) and `docker-publish.yml` (`test`, then `build-and-push`, which builds the image for both CPU types in one job, the arm64 copy under QEMU, as upstream does). Upstream's other workflows, `reset-credits.yml` and `update-contributors.yml`, run only on a schedule or a manual dispatch, so they do not run here.

**One repository per lane.** Most samples ran concurrently, each in its own cache scope (one repository per lane: `benchmark-prompts.chat-lane1` to `benchmark-prompts.chat-lane3`, with the same branches, events and payloads as this repository), so their caches never mix; a cold sample ran with no caches in its repository. 3 of the 10 samples on this page (GitHub-hosted runners round 1, and StarSling Runners (with agents) rounds 1 and 2) came from an earlier sequential run of the same configuration in this repository, one sample at a time; the other 7 came from the lanes. Their runs are linked in the sample table.

**Root and non-root StarSling jobs.** At about 11:13 AM PST on 2026-11-16, StarSling switched this organization's jobs from root to an ordinary (non-root) user. Samples are classed by their first workflow start. Every StarSling sample in this benchmark started after the switch: all 10 StarSling samples (the 5 shown here and the 5 of the control) ran as the ordinary user, so no root samples are pooled.

**RAM-disk storage.** This benchmark counts StarSling samples only when every StarSling runner had its usual RAM disk. After a storage change in this organization, every StarSling sample's runners were checked; none was voided for storage, and no sample on this page was replaced.

**Collector fix.** The collector that reads each image build log was fixed during the benchmark. With the agent PR, BuildKit runs the shared amd64 `npm ci` once and prints it under either the `deps` or the `build-deps` stage (one lane 3 sample printed only `deps`), so the collector now also recognises the fix by the builder's `COPY --from=build-deps`, and credits the one Next.js build to both images. The check names are the same with and without the fix. The record this page uses was built with the fixed collector.

**Bench-only changes, identical in every configuration and never part of the agent PR:**
  - Switched off: the `Log in to Container Registry` step (`if: false`; upstream has no condition on it). It only serves the image upload, and nothing may be published from here.
  - Image upload off: the `Build and push Docker image` step runs with `push: false` instead of `push: true`. Both CPU images are still built, and the BuildKit cache is still read and written; only the final upload to the registry is skipped. Upstream's step did upload both images on this merge, so that work is not in any column.
  - Time limit: the benchmark waits up to 90 minutes for a sample (the default is 60; upstream's own `docker-publish.yml` run of this merge took 38 minutes, and GitHub-hosted samples here took up to 55). This is a wait limit only; nothing measured changes.
  - Runner labels: upstream's `ubuntu-latest` (Ubuntu 24.04 at the pinned commit) is replaced by the runner label of each configuration (see Runner sizes).
  - One harness step, `Benchmark event context (harness)`, is added at the start of every job. It prints two IDs so each job can be matched to its sample; its median time is 0 s.
  - On the agent PR's own branch (`starsling/develop`) only, never in a replay: a setup commit points both workflows' triggers at that branch and their runners at StarSling, and applies the same login and upload switch-off, so the PR's checks run there.

**Runner sizes.** Upstream's `ubuntu-latest` jobs run on GitHub `ubuntu-24.04-4core` (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) and StarSling `starsling-ubuntu-24.04` (4 vCPU, 16 GiB). StarSling's 4 vCPU runners can burst to 5 vCPU and 32 GB RAM (Afterburner); GitHub's 4-core runners have 16 GB. Every job in this merge runs on those labels. The linux/arm64 image is built under QEMU emulation on these x64 runners in every configuration, as upstream does. In every counted sample, no job waited more than 12 s for a runner.

**Upstream reference (context only; not like-for-like; not the headline).** What upstream sees today: a median 35.0 min per merge to the default branch on upstream's own GitHub runners (n=12, most recent comparable merges to the default branch within the last 60 days; standard runners, warm caches, many commits; includes image push; not a like-for-like replay).

agentPrs.summary: Builds the Next.js app once, on the runner's own CPU, instead of once per CPU type with the arm64 copy under CPU emulation (QEMU). One file, `docker/Dockerfile`: a new dependency and build stage runs `npm ci` and `npm run build` on the build machine's platform; native files for that platform are removed from the build output, and the final image restores the target CPU's Prisma client from its own dependency stage. The workflow is untouched: the `test` job still gates the image, and the image's runtime `npm install --no-save prisma@6.19 dotenv` is unchanged.

whatWasSlow: Every merge to prompts.chat's default branch runs two workflows. `ci.yml` runs one `Test` job (a median 108 s on GitHub-hosted runners). `docker-publish.yml` runs the tests again in its own `test` job (97 s), then one `build-and-push` job that builds the Docker image for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. That one job is almost the whole wait: it took a median 3,050 s of the 3,154 s merge on GitHub-hosted runners, 2,987 s of it in the `Build and push Docker image` step. Without the fix, the image build installs the dependencies and runs the Next.js build once per CPU type, and the arm64 copy runs under CPU emulation (QEMU), where the build is very slow.
whatWeChanged:
The original showcase for this project proposed one fix: build the app once, natively, and reuse it for both images. We measured it on StarSling runners, with 5 runs on each side (the CI as it was, and the CI with the fix), on the step it changes. Every sample was cold.

| Fix | Result | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Build the Next.js app once, on the build machine's own CPU | `Build and push Docker image` step of the `build-and-push` job: 1,687 s to 1,314 s (median), 22.1% faster; every run with the fix beat every run without it (slowest with it 1,415 s, fastest without it 1,511 s). | Kept (agent PR 1) |

A fuller version of the fix, which also drops the duplicate `test` job and installs the Prisma CLI from the lockfile, was not used.
